doc.title: Frank Tiberi interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 30, 2022

title: What counts as a wrong note
summary: He says wrong notes come from not knowing tonality; blue notes and flat nines break the concept; minor seven flat five as Locrian.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Interesting. Are there wrong notes or unintended notes in improvising that you hear your students — let me rephrase. If you’re listening to them and they’re trying to do some of the things you’ve passed on to them, what constitutes a wrong note?

Well not being able to really know their tonality. That is the most important thing actually because you’re able to do deceptive inserts in the voice leading fashion actually, but if you don’t know your tonality that distinguishes a wrong note. If — you’ve got to be very consonant and as I say, so therefore you know if you don’t know your tonality that’s the part that I generally emphasize actually.

Okay. If you’re — forgive me for trying to get a handle on this a little more. If you’re doing one of those sort of substitutions where you’re playing for a moment a half step above the chord that’s going on, but you just used the word “consonant.” So how do those two things live together?

Well you know you don’t use the blue notes actually, you don’t use the flat nines, the — if you use them actually you’re going out of context. I mean and if you use them it should be just individually used that way. But I mean so far as the concept is concerned if you use them actually you’re in the blue notes already. As I say if you’re doing a deceptive insert but before. So therefore you have to be consonant like and just be voice leading, so this way if you do, you know if you do sharp nines or flat fives or anything like that

actually it doesn’t work, it doesn’t work. I’m talking about a particular concept now. If you do them individually certainly they work. If you play a minor seven flat five you know then you play I’ll just say the Thelonious Monk thing minor seven flat five and you know that’s a Locrian and it’s simple to really address it as a major third — major third below the dominant.
